XLK Does Not Own Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Netflix or Tesla. Three Stocks Are 35.87% of It
Millions of investors bought XLK expecting broad exposure to the companies reshaping the economy, but a closer look at its SEC filing reveals several of the most recognizable names in tech are nowhere inside it, and the ones that are…
Published October 6, 2026, 6:33pm ET · 4 min read
The ETF Examiner desk. Editor: Ryne Mauck.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
A couple intently reviews financial data on their laptop, reflecting the serious consideration investors give to their portfolios, especially when dealing with specific ETFs like XLK. © 24/7 Wall St.
If you bought a popular tech sector ETF for broad technology exposure, open its most recent SEC portfolio filing. As of June 30, 2026, the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSEARCA:XLK) held no shares of Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms, Netflix, or Tesla. In the same filing, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction), Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) made up 35.87% of the fund. The ten largest positions came to 64.45%.
That gap between what’s missing and what dominates is the fund’s main limitation for investors seeking broad tech exposure. The word “technology” on the label covers a much narrower and more concentrated piece of the market than most buyers expect.
What Your Technology Fund Actually Holds
The filing lists 74 equity positions supporting about $123.9 billion in net assets. NVIDIA led at 14.65%, Apple came next at 12.85%, and Microsoft held 8.38%. Three more chip companies each had more than 5%, and chip equipment suppliers took up most of the other top-ten spots. At the other end, dozens of positions each made up less than 0.5% of assets.
So investors expecting broad exposure to the tech economy own a portfolio driven by a small group of semiconductor and hardware companies.
Why Alphabet and Amazon Fall Outside the Fund
XLK tracks a sector index built on the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS). GICS assigns every public company to exactly one sector. It puts Alphabet, Meta, and Netflix in Communication Services and Amazon and Tesla in Consumer Discretionary. XLK only holds companies classified as Information Technology.
GICS sorts companies by how they make money. Alphabet and Meta earn most of their revenue from advertising. Amazon’s classification follows its retail operations, and Tesla’s follows its vehicle manufacturing business. That means a highly technological business can still end up in a different sector.
All of this is disclosed and standard practice. The classification is public, and the fund follows its index. The cost comes from a common habit: few buyers read the sector definition before they buy a sector fund.
Concentration Risk Behind a Sector Label
When several of the biggest tech-adjacent companies are left out, the giants that remain carry more weight. With 74 stocks and 35.87% of assets in just three of them, XLK’s results depend heavily on NVIDIA, Apple, and Microsoft. A prolonged decline in any one of them could move the whole fund more than its name suggests.
That concentration has paid off recently. XLK gained 41.07% over the year ending October 5, 2026. Concentration amplifies losses as well as gains, and a retiree who draws income from a portfolio feels the losses more. Investors who want AI exposure without piling further into the same three chip and hardware names have options beyond the semiconductor sector (we covered seven of them, from power to cooling to networking, in a free report you can grab here).
XLK won’t give you either Alphabet or Amazon. Adding an S&P 500 fund changes the math in a way many investors miss. The broad fund already owns those companies at market weight, so XLK on top mostly adds more NVIDIA, Apple, and Microsoft to a portfolio that already holds them.
It works the other way too. If you already own large stakes in any of those three companies directly, buying XLK could double your exposure.
A Broader Tech ETF Includes Alphabet and Meta
The iShares U.S. Technology ETF (NYSEARCA:IYW) tracks the Russell 1000 Technology RIC 22.5/45 Capped Index, which classifies companies differently. Its top holdings have included Alphabet and Meta Platforms. The Vanguard Information Technology ETF follows a GICS-based index. It leaves out the same companies XLK does. Check each issuer’s current factsheet for expense ratios and top-ten weights before you compare.
XLK suits investors wanting concentrated exposure to the GICS Information Technology sector (chips, hardware, and enterprise software) and comfortable with a top-heavy portfolio. XLK is the wrong product for investors seeking broad technology exposure that includes the platforms most people call Big Tech.
Keep the dates in mind. These holdings come from the June 30, 2026 SEC filing. Weights change, and index providers review classifications from time to time, so a company can be moved to a different sector. Before you buy any sector fund, read the index methodology that defines the sector. That document tells you what you actually own.

Alphabet Inc. Class A stock (ISIN US02079K3059) traded at around USD 349.54 on Nasdaq as of September 18, 2026, leaving room against an average analyst price target of USD 422.16 that implies about 20.8% upside based on recent data.
The most immediate catalyst for Alphabet A stock came on September 18, 2026, when Tigress Financial analyst Ivan Feinseth reiterated a Strong Buy rating and raised his price target to USD 485 from USD 415, underscoring confidence in the company’s artificial intelligence strategy.Yahoo Finance reports that this new target implies roughly 39.6% potential upside from the level cited in the note.
According to BigGo Finance on September 18, 2026, Tigress Financial’s reassessment builds on Alphabet’s positioning across search, YouTube and Google Cloud as AI becomes more deeply embedded in its products and infrastructure.
Recent quarterly figures highlight cloud and ad growth
Alphabet’s most recent reported quarter, the second quarter of 2026 ended in June 2026, provides the fundamental backdrop for the bullish calls.BigGo Finance notes that in Q2 2026 Alphabet generated total revenue of USD 119.8 billion, up 24% year over year and ahead of analyst expectations of USD 116.9 billion, a beat of USD 2.9 billion.
Within that total, search and other advertising revenue rose 17% to USD 63.3 billion compared with the prior year, while YouTube advertising climbed 13% to USD 11.1 billion in Q2 2026.BigGo Finance also highlights Google Cloud revenue of USD 24.8 billion in the quarter, an 82% year-over-year increase that far exceeded the roughly 64% growth Wall Street had expected.
The profitability profile of Google Cloud has shifted markedly.BigGo Finance reports that Google Cloud’s operating margin reached 35.6% in Q2 2026, up from 20.7% a year earlier, and operating income for the segment more than tripled to USD 8.8 billion.
Cloud backlog has become another key figure for investors tracking long-term demand.BigGo Finance states that Alphabet’s contracted Google Cloud backlog reached USD 514 billion in Q2 2026, increasing by USD 50 billion from the prior quarter and crossing the half-trillion mark for the first time, which underpins the bull case around future AI and cloud revenue.
The quarter was not uniformly positive.BigGo Finance notes that adjusted earnings per share in Q2 2026 came in at USD 2.85, slightly below the USD 2.89 analysts had expected, and that free cash flow in the quarter turned negative to minus USD 5.9 billion as capital expenditures doubled year over year to USD 44.9 billion.
Beyond the Tigress Financial call, the broader analyst community is constructive on Alphabet A stock.MarketBeat data as of September 18, 2026 show a consensus rating of Buy for Alphabet, based on 5 strong buy ratings, 45 buy ratings and 4 hold ratings, with no sell recommendations.
The same overview indicates an average price target of USD 422.16 for Alphabet A shares, representing about 20.8% upside from the USD 349.54 level cited as the current price in that dataset.MarketBeat lists a high analyst target of USD 515.00 and a low of USD 255.00, illustrating a wide but still bullish range of views.
According to Simply Wall St, a separate compilation of analyst forecasts shows a current average 12-month price target of around USD 432.83 versus a share price close to USD 349.68, implying roughly 23.8% upside and suggesting the stock is trading at a discount to that intrinsic estimate.
The valuation metrics help frame that upside.MarketBeat cites a trailing twelve-month earnings per share figure of USD 19.91 for Alphabet and a price-to-earnings ratio of about 17.56 at a share price of USD 349.54, which, paired with the growth rates in Q2 2026, is one reason many analysts argue the stock remains reasonably valued for a megacap technology name.
Price action, range and market capitalization
On the market side, Alphabet A stock continues to trade near the upper portion of its 52-week range.MarketBeat reports a closing price of USD 349.54 for Alphabet A shares on Nasdaq as of September 18, 2026, with a 52-week low of USD 235.84 and a 52-week high of USD 408.61.
At that USD 349.54 level, the stock trades roughly 14.4% below its 52-week high and about 48.3% above its 52-week low, giving investors a sense of how far the shares have already recovered over the past year while still leaving a gap to prior peaks.
The same data show Alphabet’s market capitalization at around USD 4.27 trillion as of September 18, 2026, with trading volume of about 47.5 million shares against an average volume of 23.03 million shares, indicating elevated interest in the name around recent news.
Shorter-term price snapshots from other portals broadly align with that picture: one overview notes that Alphabet A shares closed at USD 347.33 on September 17, 2026, before moving higher following the Tigress Financial price target increase.Financial Modeling Prep describes that closing level as supporting a market capitalization of roughly USD 4.25 trillion.
Capital spending and cash flow as key risk themes
Despite the strong revenue and cloud metrics, capital intensity and cash generation have emerged as important watchpoints for Alphabet A stock.BigGo Finance points out that capital spending doubled year over year to USD 44.9 billion in Q2 2026 as Alphabet accelerated investment in data centers and AI infrastructure, contributing to the first negative free cash flow quarter in the company’s history at minus USD 5.9 billion.
For investors, the question is how quickly those elevated investments can translate into sustainable earnings growth and cash generation, especially as AI workloads can demand ongoing capacity expansion.
Another risk factor is earnings quality versus expectations.BigGo Finance notes that Q2 2026 adjusted EPS of USD 2.85 fell slightly short of the USD 2.89 consensus despite the revenue beat, a modest miss that underscores how tightly expectations are calibrated for a company of Alphabet’s scale.
Dividend profile and shareholder returns
Alphabet has only recently added a cash dividend to its shareholder-return mix.MarketBeat notes that the company declared a quarterly dividend of USD 0.22 per share, corresponding to an annualized payout of USD 0.88 and a dividend yield of about 0.3% based on recent share prices.
The payout ratio currently stands at around 4.42%, a level that leaves Alphabet substantial flexibility to continue prioritizing reinvestment and share repurchases while gradually increasing the dividend over time if management chooses.
The next formal earnings report and any potential AI or cloud-related announcements from Alphabet will be closely watched, although recent sources in this search set do not provide a specific upcoming earnings date beyond referencing the Q2 2026 release on July 22, 2026.
Until a new quarter is reported, the combination of strong revenue growth, improving cloud margins, negative free cash flow driven by heavy capital expenditures, and an elevated AI investment cycle will likely frame how investors assess Alphabet A stock relative to its USD 422.16 consensus target and the USD 485 price goal set by Tigress Financial.

The Overlooked Winner From Google’s Free AI Video Move: Micron
Tue, October 6, 2026 at 3:08 PM PDT 5 min read
As of September 23, AI video creation in Vids no longer costs anything for Google and Workspace users. The upgrade draws on Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash, the newest addition to Google's model lineup. Videos can be generated in full high definition, with users deciding how long each clip lasts. Longer scenes can also be built without characters or lighting drifting between shots.
Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) is aiming it at small businesses and marketers, offering templates for those without editing experience. Every clip carries a hidden SynthID watermark. The move expands on an April update that first brought AI video to free accounts. Google's free AI video push is part of a much broader effort to monetize AI across Search, Cloud, and advertising. We recently compared Alphabet with Amazon to see which AI cloud stock makes the stronger investment case.
The Overlooked Winner From Google's Free AI Video Move
I see this as a classic Google play. Give the tool away, build the habit, and make money around it. There are a few ways this could pay off. Free users who hit their limits can upgrade to paid AI plans, which offer far more video generations. Businesses that start using Vids are more likely to stay in Workspace instead of switching to Microsoft or Canva. And since Vids can publish straight to YouTube, more videos mean more content for Google to run ads against.
Investors weren't convinced on the day, though. Alphabet shares fell nearly 4%, although the decline came amid a broader tech selloff and cannot be clearly attributed to the Vids announcement. I think that reaction misses the bigger picture. Google has done this before with Gmail, Maps, and Android, and each one ended up strengthening its core business considerably.
Institutional interest in Alphabet had been growing even before this launch. The number of hedge funds holding the stock rose from 265 at the end of Q1 2026 to 275 by the end of Q2. Their holdings also rose from $72.4 billion to $93.7 billion.
That kind of backing gives me more confidence in Google's long-term AI strategy. So the recent dip could end up creating an entry point for investors.
Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) won't get a mention in Google's announcement, and most investors wouldn't see a link between the two either. But I think it's one of the quieter winners here. AI video generation is computationally intensive and can increase demand for accelerator memory, including high-bandwidth memory, where Micron is one of the major suppliers. The demand also builds faster than it seems. It's rare to get the perfect clip on the first try, so most users will run the same prompt again and again, drawing on that memory each time.
Micron's Valuation Assumes the Boom Won't Last
Micron's valuation reflects the cyclical nature of the memory business. The forward P/E of 7x has no meaningful 5-year average to compare against, since Micron's loss in 2023 distorts the history. On its own, though, it looks fairly inexpensive for a business growing rapidly. The EPS outlook suggests that Wall Street does not expect the boom to last. Analysts expect earnings to grow 128% in fiscal 2027, which is exceptional since it comes on top of a record year. The earnings then slow down to a growth of just 9% in 2028, before falling 23% and 67% over the next two years. It is clear that Wall Street thinks these high margins and sales are not sustainable, either because supply will catch up or because an improvement in technology will resolve the memory bottleneck. We made a case for this previously, debating whether this Micron cycle is different.
Micron has plenty of financial flexibility too, with $38.36 billion in cash and equivalents and another $5.07 billion in short-term investments, against roughly $5.18 billion in total debt. If everyday AI tools keep demand steady, those later estimates could prove too conservative. Despite trading at a forward earnings multiple that looks like an anomaly, there is one stock that has even stronger revenue growth and operates in an emerging technology. You can read about it in our 10 High Beta Stocks With Strong Revenue Growth.
What interests me more is how this fits the bigger debate around Micron. The main worry is that memory demand depends heavily on a handful of big tech companies building data centers. If they slow spending, the cycle turns, and analysts already expect Micron's earnings to fall sharply by 2029. Free tools like Vids give those companies a stronger reason to keep buying, since the demand now comes from millions of everyday users. Steady usage like this is exactly what could help the cycle run longer than many expect.
Micron has seen an even sharper jump in hedge fund interest. The number of funds holding the stock rose from 154 at the end of Q1 2026 to 184 by the end of Q2. The value of their holdings more than doubled from $14.3 billion to $34.9 billion, partly helped by Micron's rising share price.
Hedge funds already seem to be betting on a longer memory cycle. If consumer AI tools keep spreading, that bet looks increasingly reasonable to me.
While we acknowledge the potential of MU as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. Alphabet Inc. Class A stock (ISIN US02079K3059) closed at USD 347.33 on Nasdaq on September 17, 2026, up 1.3 percent from the prior close and reflecting renewed confidence in the company’s search and artificial intelligence strategy. As recent analyst commentary on September 18, 2026 highlights, Wall Street is increasingly pricing in further upside for Alphabet’s core businesses and new AI products.
Analysts raise targets on search and AI strength
According to Invezz on September 18, 2026, one Wall Street analyst lifted their price target on Alphabet to USD 450 from USD 420, implying more than 30 percent upside versus Alphabet A stock’s close on September 17, 2026. Separately, Invezz reports that Tigress Financial Partners raised its target to USD 485 from USD 415 while maintaining a Strong Buy view, pointing to an upside of more than 40 percent relative to Alphabet A’s latest closing price.
These target increases build on the broader consensus view. Based on data cited by MarketBeat on September 18, 2026, Alphabet A stock carries a consensus Buy rating and an average target price of USD 422.16, suggesting that analysts as a group see roughly 21.5 percent upside from the September 17, 2026 close of USD 347.33. For investors, this clustering of targets in the low to mid USD 400 range signals confidence that Alphabet can sustain high double-digit earnings and cash flow growth.
Recent quarterly figures show strong growth and high margins
Alphabet’s latest reported quarter provides the fundamental backdrop for these optimistic calls. According to quarterly data summarized by MarketBeat on September 17, 2026, Alphabet reported earnings per share of USD 9.11 in its most recent quarter, far above the consensus estimate of USD 2.89 and representing a beat of USD 6.22 per share. Revenue for the same quarter reached USD 119.80 billion, exceeding analyst expectations of USD 117.07 billion and marking a 24.2 percent increase compared with the prior-year quarter.
These numbers underscore the profitability of Alphabet’s business model. As MarketBeat notes, Alphabet posted a net margin of 54.77 percent and a return on equity of 51.32 percent in that quarter, pointing to very efficient use of capital. On a full-year view, equities research analysts expect Alphabet to deliver about USD 20.52 in earnings per share for the current fiscal year, reinforcing the narrative of robust earnings power.
Alphabet has also moved into the camp of dividend-paying technology giants. The company recently paid a quarterly dividend of USD 0.22 per share on September 14, 2026 to shareholders of record on September 7, 2026, according to figures cited by MarketBeat. On an annualized basis that amounts to USD 0.88 per share, corresponding to a dividend yield of about 0.3 percent and a payout ratio of 4.42 percent, leaving most of Alphabet’s cash flow available for reinvestment and share repurchases.
Market reaction and valuation context for Alphabet A stock
The strong fundamental picture has been reflected in recent price action. Alphabet A stock closed at USD 342.87 on Nasdaq on the prior trading day and then rose 1.3 percent to USD 347.33 on September 17, 2026, with intraday trading reaching as high as USD 349.50 and volume of 19,035,059 shares, according to MarketBeat. Pre-market quotations on September 18, 2026 showed Alphabet A around USD 354.90, indicating that investors were initially willing to extend the advance.
Price snapshots from portals such as Yahoo Finance on September 18, 2026 list Alphabet A at USD 347.33, up about 1.30 percent, and Alphabet’s Class C shares at USD 343.68, up around 1.27 percent. This pairing suggests that the entire Alphabet equity complex benefited from the latest analyst optimism and broader market recovery after a short losing streak.
Valuation metrics are shaped by both the share price and the earnings trajectory. While the most recent market capitalization figure is not explicitly cited in these week-filtered sources, the combination of a USD 347.33 share price and forecast full-year EPS of about USD 20.52 implies a forward price-earnings multiple in the mid-teens. For a company growing revenue by 24.2 percent year over year and maintaining net margins above 50 percent, that earnings multiple is central to the bullish case that Alphabet A stock still offers room for re-rating as AI-related revenues scale.
Risks and what could challenge the bullish thesis
Despite the positive sentiment, analysts and investors continue to watch several risk factors that could affect Alphabet A stock. Legal and regulatory scrutiny remains an ongoing theme: recent articles on Yahoo Finance on September 18, 2026 highlight how securities class actions and capital claims can weigh on large technology names, and Alphabet appears among the trending tickers in that context. For Alphabet, such issues may manifest in higher compliance costs, potential fines or constraints on certain business practices, all of which could dampen margin expansion.
Competition in search and AI is another structural risk. While the latest quarter shows Alphabet expanding revenue by more than 20 percent and beating earnings expectations by over USD 6 per share, rivals are also investing heavily to capture AI workloads and digital advertising budgets. If alternative platforms gain share or regulators limit how Alphabet deploys user data for personalized ads and AI models, the projected revenue growth embedded in price targets of USD 422.16, USD 450 and USD 485 could prove optimistic.
Finally, the broader market backdrop matters. As TechFlowPost reported on September 18, 2026, US equities recently ended a three-session losing streak, with Alphabet A noted at USD 347.33, up 1.30 percent on that day, alongside other gainers. Should risk appetite reverse again due to macroeconomic shocks or interest-rate worries, high-valuation growth stocks such as Alphabet could see price pressure even if company-specific fundamentals stay strong.
Next dates and investor takeaway for Alphabet A stock
Alphabet’s investor relations calendar on Alphabet provides the schedule for upcoming events, including future quarterly earnings releases and shareholder meetings, although specific next dates are not detailed in the week-filtered sources reviewed here. What is clear from the latest quarter and the September 18, 2026 analyst actions is that investors will be focusing closely on how quickly Alphabet can translate its AI investments into sustained revenue and margin gains.
In summary, Alphabet A stock stands at USD 347.33 as of the Nasdaq close on September 17, 2026, with consensus and selected bullish analysts seeing potential for the share price to move toward or above the USD 400 mark based on strong recent earnings and rapid top-line growth. For retail investors, the combination of high profitability, a modest dividend, and aggressive AI-driven expansion makes Alphabet A one of the central names to watch in large-cap technology.

If you bought a popular tech sector ETF for broad technology exposure, open its most recent SEC portfolio filing. As of June 30, 2026, the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSEARCA:XLK) held no shares of Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms, Netflix, or Tesla. In the same filing, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction), Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) made up 35.87% of the fund. The ten largest positions came to 64.45%.
That gap between what’s missing and what dominates is the fund’s main limitation for investors seeking broad tech exposure. The word “technology” on the label covers a much narrower and more concentrated piece of the market than most buyers expect.
What Your Technology Fund Actually Holds
The filing lists 74 equity positions supporting about $123.9 billion in net assets. NVIDIA led at 14.65%, Apple came next at 12.85%, and Microsoft held 8.38%. Three more chip companies each had more than 5%, and chip equipment suppliers took up most of the other top-ten spots. At the other end, dozens of positions each made up less than 0.5% of assets.
So investors expecting broad exposure to the tech economy own a portfolio driven by a small group of semiconductor and hardware companies.
Why Alphabet and Amazon Fall Outside the Fund
XLK tracks a sector index built on the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS). GICS assigns every public company to exactly one sector. It puts Alphabet, Meta, and Netflix in Communication Services and Amazon and Tesla in Consumer Discretionary. XLK only holds companies classified as Information Technology.
GICS sorts companies by how they make money. Alphabet and Meta earn most of their revenue from advertising. Amazon’s classification follows its retail operations, and Tesla’s follows its vehicle manufacturing business. That means a highly technological business can still end up in a different sector.
All of this is disclosed and standard practice. The classification is public, and the fund follows its index. The cost comes from a common habit: few buyers read the sector definition before they buy a sector fund.
Concentration Risk Behind a Sector Label
When several of the biggest tech-adjacent companies are left out, the giants that remain carry more weight. The Overlooked Winner From Google’s Free AI Video Move: Micron
Tue, October 6, 2026 at 3:08 PM PDT 5 min read
As of September 23, AI video creation in Vids no longer costs anything for Google and Workspace users. The upgrade draws on Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash, the newest addition to Google's model lineup. Videos can be generated in full high definition, with users deciding how long each clip lasts. Longer scenes can also be built without characters or lighting drifting between shots.
Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) is aiming it at small businesses and marketers, offering templates for those without editing experience. Every clip carries a hidden SynthID watermark. The move expands on an April update that first brought AI video to free accounts. Google's free AI video push is part of a much broader effort to monetize AI across Search, Cloud, and advertising. We recently compared Alphabet with Amazon to see which AI cloud stock makes the stronger investment case.
The Overlooked Winner From Google's Free AI Video Move
I see this as a classic Google play. Give the tool away, build the habit, and make money around it. There are a few ways this could pay off. Free users who hit their limits can upgrade to paid AI plans, which offer far more video generations. Businesses that start using Vids are more likely to stay in Workspace instead of switching to Microsoft or Canva. And since Vids can publish straight to YouTube, more videos mean more content for Google to run ads against.
Investors weren't convinced on the day, though. Alphabet shares fell nearly 4%, although the decline came amid a broader tech selloff and cannot be clearly attributed to the Vids announcement. I think that reaction misses the bigger picture. Google has done this before with Gmail, Maps, and Android, and each one ended up strengthening its core business considerably.
Institutional interest in Alphabet had been growing even before this launch. The number of hedge funds holding the stock rose from 265 at the end of Q1 2026 to 275 by the end of Q2. Their holdings also rose from $72.4 billion to $93.7 billion.
That kind of backing gives me more confidence in Google's long-term AI strategy. So the recent dip could end up creating an entry point for investors.
Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) won't get a mention in Google's announcement, and most investors wouldn't see a link between the two either. But I think it's one of the quieter winners here. AI video generation is computationally intensive and can increase demand for accelerator memory, including high-bandwidth memory, where Micron is one of the major suppliers. The demand also builds faster than it seems. It's rare to get the perfect clip on the first try, so most users will run the same prompt again and again, drawing on that memory each time.
Micron's Valuation Assumes the Boom Won't Last
Micron's valuation reflects the cyclical nature of the memory business. The forward P/E of 7x has no meaningful 5-year average to compare against, since Micron's loss in 2023 distorts the history. On its own, though, it looks fairly inexpensive for a business growing rapidly. The EPS outlook suggests that Wall Street does not expect the boom to last. Analysts expect earnings to grow 128% in fiscal 2027, which is exceptional since it comes on top of a record year. The earnings then slow down to a growth of just 9% in 2028, before falling 23% and 67% over the next two years. It is clear that Wall Street thinks these high margins and sales are not sustainable, either because supply will catch up or because an improvement in technology will resolve the memory bottleneck. We made a case for this previously, debating whether this Micron cycle is different.
Micron has plenty of financial flexibility too, with $38.36 billion in cash and equivalents and another $5.07 billion in short-term investments, against roughly $5.18 billion in total debt. If everyday AI tools keep demand steady, those later estimates could prove too conservative. Despite trading at a forward earnings multiple that looks like an anomaly, there is one stock that has even stronger revenue growth and operates in an emerging technology. You can read about it in our 10 High Beta Stocks With Strong Revenue Growth.
What interests me more is how this fits the bigger debate around Micron. The main worry is that memory demand depends heavily on a handful of big tech companies building data centers. If they slow spending, the cycle turns, and analysts already expect Micron's earnings to fall sharply by 2029. Free tools like Vids give those companies a stronger reason to keep buying, since the demand now comes from millions of everyday users. Steady usage like this is exactly what could help the cycle run longer than many expect.
Micron has seen an even sharper jump in hedge fund interest. The number of funds holding the stock rose from 154 at the end of Q1 2026 to 184 by the end of Q2. The value of their holdings more than doubled from $14.3 billion to $34.9 billion, partly helped by Micron's rising share price.
Hedge funds already seem to be betting on a longer memory cycle. If consumer AI tools keep spreading, that bet looks increasingly reasonable to me.
